title: Unlocking Japan’s low-carbon future: asymmetric effects of technological innovation, and economic growth on carbon emissions
summary: Japan's pursuit of carbon neutrality by 2050 faces the persistent challenge of reconciling economic expansion and international trade with sustained reductions in carbon emissions. Although technological innovation and natural resources are
content: Japan's pursuit of carbon neutrality by 2050 faces the persistent challenge of reconciling economic expansion and international trade with sustained reductions in carbon emissions. Although technological innovation and natural resources are increasingly recognized as important determinants of environmental quality, existing evidence provides limited insight into whether positive and negative changes in these factors generate different environmental outcomes. This study examines the asymmetric effects of technological innovation and natural resources on CO₂ emissions in Japan using annual data from 1980 to 2020. The study employs the Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) model and dynamic asymmetric multiplier analysis to distinguish short- and long-run effects. The results confirm a stable long-run relationship among the variables. Economic growth and trade openness significantly increase CO₂ emissions in both the short and long run. Conversely, positive technological innovation significantly reduces emissions in both periods, while negative technological shocks increase emissions in the short run. Positive changes in natural resources also reduce emissions in the long run. The findings highlight the importance of sustained technological progress, efficient resource management, and low-carbon economic and trade strategies for Japan's decarbonization.

title: A Charge-Consistent Long-Range Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential Compatible with Quantum Linear System Algorithms
source: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
summary: Abstract Charge equilibration in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) requires repeatedly solving linear systems, providing a promising target for quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs). However, conventional electronegativity e
content: Abstract Charge equilibration in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) requires repeatedly solving linear systems, providing a promising target for quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs). However, conventional electronegativity equalization schemes suffer from spurious fractional charges between neutral fragments at large separations. To address this limitation, we incorporate atom-condensed Kohn–Sham density functional theory approximated to second order (ACKS2) into a long-range equivariant neural-network MLIP. Across benchmark systems, the ACKS2-based model improves energy, force, and charge predictions. At a molecule–metal interface, ACKS2 restores molecular fragments to near-neutral charge states upon separation while preserving local charge redistribution near adsorption. Because ACKS2 charge equilibration reduces to solving a linear system, the classical solver can be directly replaced with the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm during inference, demonstrating compatibility with quantum linear-system solvers. These results indicate that ACKS2 provides a promising framework for charge-aware MLIPs and highlight a potential pathway toward atomistic simulations based on QLSAs.

title: LoKI-GM: a global model framework for plasma chemistry studies
summary: Abstract Global (zero-dimensional or spatially averaged) models are widely employed to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas (LTPs). By adopting a spatially average description of the plasma, they substantially reduce the com
content: Abstract Global (zero-dimensional or spatially averaged) models are widely employed to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas (LTPs). By adopting a spatially average description of the plasma, they substantially reduce the computational cost while still providing reliable and detailed insight into the key processes taking place in the plasma. In their most general formulation, global models involve the coupled solution of a Boltzmann solver (to describe the electron kinetics) and a Chemistry solver (to describe the heavy-species kinetics). This paper presents a tutorial on the LisbOn Kinetics Global Model (LoKI-GM) framework, developed in MATLAB and available as open-source code. The framework couples the Boltzmann solver LoKI-B, which solves the space-independent form of the two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetised non-equilibrium LTPs, excited by DC/HF electric fields or time-dependent (non-oscillatory) electric fields, and the Chemistry solver LoKI-C, which solves the system of zero-dimensional rate balance equations for the main charged and neutral species in the plasma and at the surface, receiving as input the kinetic schemes for the gas/plasma/surface system under study. Distinctive features of LoKI-GM include the closure of the model through charge neutrality, which yields the self-consistent maintenance field of DC and HF discharges, and the availability of several transport models for charged and neutral species. LoKI-GM can also couple a microkinetic mesoscopic surface model and a gas thermal model to the volume kinetics. We briefly present the formulation of LoKI-GM, including its numerical solution strategy, input/output parameters, and calculation workflow for both active discharges and afterglow plasmas. The main differences with respect to existing global models are highlighted, and the flexibility of the code for plasma chemistry studies is demonstrated through representative simulation results obtained across a range of gas discharge configurations and operating conditions.

title: Geoeconomic fragmentation and the erosion of TRIPS flexibilities in technology access and distributive justice in the Global South
summary: The rise of geoeconomic fragmentation and techno-nationalism is fundamentally reshaping the global intellectual property (IP) regime. While the TRIPS Agreement was originally presented as a carefully balanced bargain that preserved flexibil
content: The rise of geoeconomic fragmentation and techno-nationalism is fundamentally reshaping the global intellectual property (IP) regime. While the TRIPS Agreement was originally presented as a carefully balanced bargain that preserved flexibilities for developing countries, contemporary security-driven export controls, investment screening, industrial subsidies, and strategic technology restrictions are increasingly constraining those flexibilities. This paper critically examines how the securitisation of technology and the weaponisation of supply chains are constraining the effective policy space of Global South countries to access, adapt, and diffuse critical technologies in pharmaceuticals, green energy, digital infrastructure, and artificial intelligence. Drawing on international trade law, political economy, and distributive justice frameworks, the paper analyses the interplay between TRIPS Articles 7, 8, 31, and 66.2 and the expanding use of national security exceptions. The paper distinguishes the continuing legal availability of those flexibilities from the material capacity to convert them into productive outcomes. Export controls, investment screening and restricted complementary assets do not amend the treaty text; they constrain its effective exercise. It argues that the current trajectory risks widening the gap between de jure intellectual-property policy space and de facto technological agency, and thereby converting IP from a development tool into an instrument of technological hierarchy and proposes pathways for reclaiming regulatory sovereignty and reconstructing a more equitable technology governance architecture in a multipolar world.

title: Palladium nanoparticles embedded in polyphenylene oxide as a simple multifunctional and recyclable platform for hydrogen production from formic acid, nitroarene reduction and tandem transfer hydrogenation
summary: Palladium nanoparticles embedded in poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (PdNPs-PPO) were developed as a simple, recyclable, and multifunctional Pd/polymer platform for hydrogen-generation and hydrogen-transfer catalysis. The catalyst was
content: Palladium nanoparticles embedded in poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (PdNPs-PPO) were developed as a simple, recyclable, and multifunctional Pd/polymer platform for hydrogen-generation and hydrogen-transfer catalysis. The catalyst was prepared by polymer swelling, Pd precursor incorporation, chemical reduction, and precipitation, affording ca. 5 nm Pd nanoparticles distributed within the PPO matrix. WAXD and TEM/FFT confirmed crystalline Pd(0) domains, whereas XPS indicated oxidized Pd species at the outermost surface. PdNPs-PPO efficiently catalyzed the NaBH 4 -mediated reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline. At a nitrobenzene/Pd molar ratio of 1000, quantitative conversion and >99% selectivity were obtained at 70 °C in 1 h, corresponding to a TOF of 1000 h -1 . In a PTFE-lined pressure reactor, quantitative aniline formation was achieved at 100 °C within 5 min, corresponding to an average TOF of 12,000 h -1 . The catalyst also promoted base-free formic acid dehydrogenation in water, selectively producing H 2 and CO 2 without detectable CO and reaching TOF values up to 620 h -1 . Formic-acid-mediated transfer hydrogenation afforded quantitative aniline formation with >99% selectivity in diethyl carbonate at 100 °C within 1 h. Higher substrate loadings increased the average TOF up to 530 h -1 , although with reduced conversion and selectivity. The apparent activation parameters derived from fixed-time catalytic data showed markedly different profiles for NaBH 4 reduction, formic acid dehydrogenation, and transfer hydrogenation. These differences are consistent with distinct surface-controlled regimes and suggest that formic-acid-derived hydrogen species participate directly in nitrobenzene reduction, although a contribution from molecular H 2 cannot be excluded. Overall, PdNPs-PPO provides an accessible and reusable platform for nitroarene reduction, selective hydrogen production, and integrated hydrogen-transfer chemistry.

title: Transitioning to low-carbon agriculture: Institutional misalignment and constraints in South Africa’s extension systems
summary: Despite climate-mitigation commitments in the global South, an implementation gap constrains sustainable agricultural development in South Africa. This study examines government extension practitioners' perceptions of climate-aligned practi
content: Despite climate-mitigation commitments in the global South, an implementation gap constrains sustainable agricultural development in South Africa. This study examines government extension practitioners' perceptions of climate-aligned practices to identify the institutional factors driving this divide. A qualitative content analysis of 1775 thematic segments from focus groups with 52 extension officers across eight provinces in 2025 reveals deep institutional misalignment. Only 10.7% of coded segments explicitly framed agriculture as a mitigation strategy, while 35.8% prioritize economic optimization and livelihood conservation. Provincial focus on climate mitigation ranges from 20.3% in Mpumalanga to 4.7% in Gauteng. Crucially, land tenure insecurity emerges as a foundational structural constraint that contributes to this misalignment by discouraging long-term climate investment. While national mandates conceptualize mitigation through global carbon accounting, local extension systems prioritize immediate economic survival. Therefore, achieving national targets requires reforming communal land governance alongside extension mandates, rather than merely introducing technical solutions. The study demonstrates that land governance reform is a prerequisite, rather than a complementary measure, for effective climate policy implementation. It advances frameworks that leverage smart technologies for carbon measurement, youth-led data management, and carbon credits, reframing mitigation as a viable economic strategy for a sustainable, low-carbon future.

title: Technology pathway choices and lifecycle costs of chinese power battery firms under carbon constraints: An empirical analysis of managerial decision-making
summary: China's power battery industry has grown into the world's largest by volume, yet firms now face mounting pressure from carbon pricing mechanisms and evolving emissions trading scheme (ETS) regulations. Strategic technology pathway choices a
content: China's power battery industry has grown into the world's largest by volume, yet firms now face mounting pressure from carbon pricing mechanisms and evolving emissions trading scheme (ETS) regulations. Strategic technology pathway choices among lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel manganese cobalt (NMC), and emerging solid-state chemistries carry material consequences for long-run manufacturing cost structures. This study investigates how carbon constraint intensity and carbon price volatility shape firm-level technology pathway decisions in listed Chinese battery manufacturers, and how managerial characteristics moderate these effects. Using an unbalanced panel of 68 listed Chinese battery firms over 2013–2022 (N = 680 firm-year observations) drawn from CSMAR, Wind, CNIPA, MIIT, and MEEB databases, we construct a Technology Pathway Index (TPI) and a Solid-State Investment Index (SSII). Carbon Constraint Intensity (CCI) combines ETS provincial coverage with prevailing carbon prices. We estimate dynamic panel models with firm and year fixed effects, supplementing OLS estimates with two-stage least squares (2SLS) using provincial energy-sector ETS coverage as an instrument. A one standard deviation increase in CCI raises TPI by 4.19 points under OLS and 5.87 points under 2SLS, confirming a robust positive effect. Carbon price volatility independently elevates solid-state investment. TMT educational diversity amplifies the CCI-TPI relationship (interaction coefficient +2.03, p = 0.004), while CEO tenure attenuates solid-state commitment under uncertainty. Higher TPI values are associated with measurable lifecycle unit cost declines, with the interaction of TPI and CCI generating an additional −0.007 log-unit reduction in COGS per year. Effects are stronger among privately owned enterprises (POEs) than state-owned enterprises (SOEs). Carbon regulation acts as a directional signal that steers managerially capable firms toward lower-carbon LFP pathways and increments solid-state R&D commitment. Policy design should account for SOE soft-budget heterogeneity, and carbon markets benefit from price stability to unlock long-horizon solid-state transitions.

title: DMSPFF: A deep multi-scale perceptual fusion framework for short-term wind power forecasting
summary: Accurate short-term wind-power forecasting supports power-system operation, but wind-power sequences combine slowly varying regimes, abrupt ramps, and non-stationary scale-dependent oscillations. Existing models often emphasize one scale or
content: Accurate short-term wind-power forecasting supports power-system operation, but wind-power sequences combine slowly varying regimes, abrupt ramps, and non-stationary scale-dependent oscillations. Existing models often emphasize one scale or use fixed feature fusion, limiting their ability to model interactions among long-term context, recent dynamics, and time–frequency patterns. This study proposes a deep multi-scale perceptual fusion framework (DMSPFF). Parallel HiPPO-LegS, sLSTM, and CWT-CNN branches encode long-term memory, short-term dynamics, and localized time–frequency structure, respectively. Transformer-based attention refines interactions between long-term and time–frequency representations before their integration with short-term features. Experiments on a German meteorological and wind-power dataset evaluate 10-, 30-, 60-, and 120-min horizons against recurrent, tree-based, kernel-based, and representative recent Transformer models. At 120 min, DMSPFF achieves R 2 = 0.88 and MAE = 3.55 kW, versus the best baseline R 2 of 0.79 and the best MAE baseline of 4.80 kW, reducing MAE by 26.0%. Wind-speed-stratified evaluation supports within-dataset robustness; two-sided Diebold–Mariano tests indicate significantly lower squared-error loss in 45 of 48 comparisons at the 5% level. These results support coordinated multi-scale representation learning for longer-horizon wind-power forecasting and operational decision-making.

title: Trace Element Transfer and Distribution in the Rock-Soil-Plant System: La Oriental Mine, Uruguay
summary: The study of systems associated with mining activities is essential to understand the transfer of trace elements from the lithosphere to the biota. This research evaluated the origin and availability of metals in the Mina La Oriental area,
content: The study of systems associated with mining activities is essential to understand the transfer of trace elements from the lithosphere to the biota. This research evaluated the origin and availability of metals in the Mina La Oriental area, in Uruguay. Rock and soil samples were collected from waste rock dumps and control sites, alongside specimens of Plantago brasiliensis, Nierembergia ericoides, and Blepharocalyx salicifolius. Results suggest that the high concentration of trace elements in soils derives from materials accumulated due to base metal mining (Cu, Pb, Zn), showing a heterogeneous distribution where Pb exhibits a lithogenic dominance associated with these waste structures. Extreme enrichment factors (EF > 40) were recorded throughout the area, exceeding the natural geochemical baseline even in locations distant from the dumps. Regarding vegetation, metal transfer was regulated by species identity: P. brasiliensis acted as an Al and Pb accumulator, whereas B. salicifolius exhibited an excluder behavior driven by effective root barriers. Meanwhile, N. ericoides showed intermediate transfer levels dependent on soil availability. Finally, cation exchange capacity, pH, and organic matter content were determined to be the primary geochemical controls of metal mobility. These findings allow for the characterization of retention mechanisms in a mining-impacted system, providing key data for the management of environmental liabilities.

title: Turning Abandoned Mines into Carbon Sinks: Laboratory Demonstration of CO2 Hydrate Sequestration in Cold-Region Goafs under Permafrost Conditions
summary: Abstract Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) is a key technology for carbon neutrality, but conventional CO2 geological sequestration suffers from high injection pressure, limited stability, and restricted storage space. Hydrate
content: Abstract Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) is a key technology for carbon neutrality, but conventional CO2 geological sequestration suffers from high injection pressure, limited stability, and restricted storage space. Hydrate-based CO2 sequestration offers high capacity, low cost, and intrinsic safety. This study proposes a novel in situ CO2 hydrate formation and sequestration method in coal mine goafs containing permafrost layers in cold regions. The natural low-temperature permafrost environment provides favorable conditions for hydrate formation, while goafs offer large storage space. To avoid hydrate plugging and improve engineering feasibility, a liquid-first CO2 constant-pressure supply and predissolution mode was adopted. We simulated goaf conditions at depths of 110–130 m and ∼1 MPa. Experiments tested three injection temperatures (293.15, 298.15, and 303.15 K) and five goaf temperatures (269.15–277.15 K) using tetrahydrofuran and tryptophan as promoters. Results proved efficient sequestration at a low pressure of 1 MPa. Under optimal conditions (injection temperature of 298.15 K, goaf temperature of 271.15 K), capacity reached 60.9 mmol of CO2/mol of water (mmol/mol) with an efficiency of 135.36 (kg·m–3)/MPa. The 26.7 h stability experiments under depressurization showed 4.21–16.09 mmol/mol dissociated initially, but 66.38%–90.77% CO2 remained sequestered. Further, one-month tests under the pressure-release condition revealed hydrate dissociation almost stopped after day 1, yielding a 65.32% permanent sequestration ratio. Crucially, under the pressure-maintained condition, the system continued to form CO2 hydrates over the 30-day period, resulting in an additional 31.04% CO2 storage. These results validate the feasibility and long-term stability of this novel approach.

title: Risk Mitigation Instruments and Investment Flows into Renewable Energy Projects in Kenya
source: International Journal of Social Science and Humanities Research (IJSSHR)
summary: Risk mitigation instruments are financial and contractual mechanisms that reduce investors’ exposure to uncertainty and potential losses in capital-intensive projects. They have become central to renewable energy financing because they redi
content: Risk mitigation instruments are financial and contractual mechanisms that reduce investors’ exposure to uncertainty and potential losses in capital-intensive projects. They have become central to renewable energy financing because they redistribute risk, stabilise expected returns and improve project bankability. In Kenya, more than 80% of electricity is generated from renewable sources, yet investment flows into the sector remain uneven and below potential because of exchange rate volatility, regulatory uncertainty, high upfront capital costs and long payback periods. Evidence on how individual instruments translate into actual investment remains limited. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the influence of risk mitigation instruments on investment flows into renewable energy projects in Kenya. It explored four instruments, namely credit guarantees, insurance mechanisms, currency hedging instruments and blended finance instruments. The study was anchored on Modern Portfolio Theory, Agency Theory, Financial Intermediation Theory and Risk Management Theory. The study adopted a descriptive and explanatory research design and targeted the 22 registered Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) renewable energy projects in Kenya. A census of the projects was undertaken and two respondents, a project manager and a financial or investment officer, were purposively selected from each project, giving 44 respondents, of whom 36 returned completed questionnaires. Structured questionnaires were used to collect data. Both descriptive and inferential statistical methods were used to analyse the data, which were presented in tables and discussed. The findings revealed that the four instruments jointly explained 58.7% of the variation in investment flows. Currency hedging instruments were the strongest predictor of investment flows, followed by credit guarantees and insurance mechanisms, while blended finance instruments had a significant but comparatively weaker influence. The study, therefore, recommends that the government, financial institutions and development partners expand accessible and affordable currency hedging products, adequately resourced credit guarantee schemes and project-specific insurance products, and strengthen blended finance frameworks through better institutional coordination and transparent risk-sharing arrangements.

title: Energy Supply in the CETO2026 Scenario – A high detail, policy-oriented deep-decarbonization scenario for the EU
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This study presents the energy supply findings of the POTEnCIA CETO 2026 Scenario, a technology-driven, policy-oriented pathway for deep decarbonization of the EU energy system in strict compliance with the European Climate Law (ECL). Devel
content: This study presents the energy supply findings of the POTEnCIA CETO 2026 Scenario, a technology-driven, policy-oriented pathway for deep decarbonization of the EU energy system in strict compliance with the European Climate Law (ECL). Developed using the POTEnCIA hybrid partial equilibrium model, the scenario integrates the latest National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs), EU-wide regulatory instruments, and techno-economic assumptions aligned with the European Commission's 2040 Climate Target framework. Historical calibration draws on the JRC Integrated Database of the European Energy System (JRC-IDEES), with 2023 as the base year. The scenario rests on three pillars: legislative frameworks, historical data calibration, and techno-economic assumptions. The ECL mandates a 55% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions relative to 1990 levels by 2030, an 85% reduction by 2040, and net-zero by 2050. Combining these targets with a system-wide carbon value drives rapid electrification and efficiency gains across all end-use sectors. Total electricity demand more than doubles between 2023 and 2050 reaching over 6000 TWh, driven primarily by electrolytic hydrogen production and road transport electrification. Coal is fully phased out by 2030, while wind and solar expand to supply 75% of electricity generation by 2050. Nuclear remains significant in line with national plans, and natural gas continues to manage renewable intermittency. Electrolytic hydrogen demand grows to 113 Mtoe (39 Mt H₂) by 2050. Initially concentrated in refineries and chemicals, demand diversifies from the 2030s, with roughly 34% directed toward synthetic fuel production by 2050. Synthetic kerosene, green ammonia, and synthetic methanol account for nearly 90% of synthetic fuel output, serving aviation, shipping, and chemicals respectively. These results underscore that climate neutrality requires simultaneous, rapid scaling of renewable electricity, electrolytic hydrogen, and synthetic fuel infrastructure across the EU.

title: Fiction as Environmental Risk Communication: Climate Change, Imagination, and the Relevance of Narrative
source: Critical studies in risk and uncertainty
summary: The essay discusses fiction as a powerful form of environmental risk communication, taking as an example the planetary risk of climate change. While risk is often approached through scientific modeling and probabilistic reasoning, its narra
content: The essay discusses fiction as a powerful form of environmental risk communication, taking as an example the planetary risk of climate change. While risk is often approached through scientific modeling and probabilistic reasoning, its narrative dimensions are equally crucial for how it is perceived and communicated. Narratives, both factual and fictional, shape cultural identities, express values, and expose how risks are framed, politicized, and contested. Risk fiction transforms abstract risks into lived realities by exploring concrete risk experiences in ways that resonate with audiences both intellectually and emotionally. Engaging scholarship from social sciences risk studies, narrative theory, and ecocriticism, the essay shows how climate fiction communicates risk by dramatizing uncertainty, ethical dilemmas, and sociopolitical conflicts, revealing the entanglement of science, politics, and media, and turning abstract threats into personal stories and embodied experience. By doing so, it demonstrates how literary and cultural studies can productively expand the scope of risk research, contributing significantly to risk studies and risk theory.

title: Bank Taxation as Financial Regulation
summary: After the 2008 Financial Crisis, regulators in the United States and abroad enacted a wide range of policies designed to strengthen the financial system. Despite considering several proposed changes to the tax code, lawmakers almost exclusi
content: After the 2008 Financial Crisis, regulators in the United States and abroad enacted a wide range of policies designed to strengthen the financial system. Despite considering several proposed changes to the tax code, lawmakers almost exclusively relied on other regulatory tools. That inaction was a missed opportunity, and the consequences of that oversight persist. Tax policy is an underappreciated dimension of financial regulation. The tax code already promotes financial stability in several important ways, such as by incentivizing banks to build reserves for bad loans and recognize losses on debt securities, and by providing predictable tax treatment during crises. These provisions demonstrate that well-designed taxation can reinforce the goals of traditional financial regulation. However, this Note identifies areas where the tax code pushes banks to engage in behavior at odds with the typical goals of bank regulation. Most prominently, while many lawmakers and scholars want banks to hold more capital, the tax code’s distinct treatment of debt and equity incentivizes banks to issue less. Preferential treatment for securitized assets contributed to the securitization boom in the lead-up to the 2008 Financial Crisis and continues to push risk outside the regulatory perimeter. Additionally, the credit union tax exemption has subsidized the growth of large institutions whose activities are increasingly indistinguishable from those of taxable banks and that operate under a separate regulatory framework that is in some respects less stringent. These tensions are not inevitable, and this Note argues that bank taxation should be understood and deployed as a financial stability tool. To that end, this Note surveys several proposals that would better align bank taxation and financial regulation. Policymakers should consider three tax-based reforms: an allowance for common equity regulatory capital to reduce the bias against equity issuance, a balance sheet levy on unstable bank liabilities to force large institutions to internalize their systemic risk, and the repeal of the credit union exemption for large institutions to eliminate a competitive distortion that benefits less stringently regulated entities. Finally, this Note addresses a fourth often-discussed proposal, a financial transaction tax, which would likely undermine rather than promote financial stability and should be approached with caution. Financial regulation does not exist in a vacuum. Lawmakers and scholars can and should treat tax policy as an integral component of the financial regulatory agenda.

title: Mapping regenerative agriculture research in coffee systems (2016–2024): A scientometric analysis of soil health, microbial indicators, and thematic trends
summary: Agriculture faces significant sustainability challenges due to increasing global demand and climate change. In this context, Regenerative Agriculture (RA) has emerged as a holistic approach to revitalizing ecosystems. Despite the growth in
content: Agriculture faces significant sustainability challenges due to increasing global demand and climate change. In this context, Regenerative Agriculture (RA) has emerged as a holistic approach to revitalizing ecosystems. Despite the growth in publications, literature remains fragmented regarding concepts and indicators, especially in perennial tropical systems like coffee. This study addresses how scientific literature has interpreted and applied RA over the past decade (2016–2024), specifically in coffee production. The objective was to systematize and critically analyze current conceptual frameworks and practical applications. Methodologically, a bibliometric and systematic literature review was conducted using Web of Science and Scopus, focusing on publication trends, soil health, and microbial processes. RA focuses on enhancing soil health, biodiversity, water conservation, and climate mitigation. Unlike conventional sustainable practices, RA improves the physical, chemical, and biological properties of soil such as organic matter, microbial diversity, and carbon sequestration without compromising productivity. Soil respiration serves as a key integrative metric for carbon fluxes. Typical practices include cover cropping, reduced tillage, and integrated systems. In coffee farming, strategies like mulching, bio-inputs, and agroforestry show potential for improving soil quality. Results show that while the USA, UK, and Australia lead research, Brazil is a growing contributor. Thematic mapping reveals a focus on carbon dynamics, though microbial indicators remain underrepresented. Significant knowledge gaps in tropical regions highlight the need for research linking soil health indicators to sustainable coffee cultivation, balancing productivity, ecosystem resilience, and long-term soil biological functioning. Key words: Soil conservation; biodiversity; coffee farming; sustainability indicators.

title: Topochemical Analysis of Pine Bark toward Structure‐First Biorefineries
summary: Pine bark is an abundant, yet underutilized forestry by-product often burnt for energy, despite its rich chemical functionality. Its broader use is limited by poor processability and high heterogeneity of products obtained through conventio
content: Pine bark is an abundant, yet underutilized forestry by-product often burnt for energy, despite its rich chemical functionality. Its broader use is limited by poor processability and high heterogeneity of products obtained through conventional fractionation. Most processes employed for bark have been traditionally designed for wood, a vastly different lignocellulosic precursor. In this work, we moved beyond bulk analysis by employing a topochemical approach to understand the bark recalcitrance and structural integrity. By advanced spectroscopic imaging combined with controlled solvent treatments and macroscale integrity analysis, we provided new insights into how bark architecture governs its recalcitrance in the context of biorefineries. Bark recalcitrance largely stems from the thick outer cell walls, dominated by conjugated C═C double bonds and unsaturated carbonyl structures, that are disrupted by alkaline agents. Removal of lipophilic extractives increases the fibers' cohesion, potentially requiring more energy input for fiber liberation. Furthermore, bark structure is loosened by removing pectins and phenolics in the middle lamella and cell corners. Macroscale texture depends on the nature, not just the amount, of removed components. By understanding the roles of each component in the integrity of the bark ultrastructure, we put forward a generic structure-first concept to develop novel bark biorefineries.

title: Decarbonization pathways of energy intensive industries in an enhanced CGE framework
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Achieving EU climate neutrality requires deep decarbonization of energy-intensive industries, where emissions stem from both fuel combustion and process/feedstock use and where competitiveness pressures are high. This study quantifies the s
content: Achieving EU climate neutrality requires deep decarbonization of energy-intensive industries, where emissions stem from both fuel combustion and process/feedstock use and where competitiveness pressures are high. This study quantifies the socio-economic implications of industrial decarbonization in the European Union to 2050, focusing on three energy-intensive sectors and using the GEM-E3 computable general equilibrium (CGE) model. We extend GEM-E3 with (i) a technology-rich, bottom-up representation of steelmaking that captures alternative production routes, input requirements, costs, and material constraints, and (ii) a dedicated module for carbon capture and storage (CCS) uptake in industrial process emissions (steel, cement, chemicals). We evaluate two policy settings: a Frozen Policy Pathway (continuation of pre-2023 EU ETS policies and limited ambition) and a Core Policy Scenario aligned with Fit-for-55 and long-term climate-neutrality objectives, including updated ETS1/ETS2, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and CO₂ standards for vehicles; variants explore sensitivity to electricity prices. Results indicate that near-complete decarbonization of energy-intensive industries by 2050 is technically achievable, but economic outcomes depend strongly on policy design and energy-system conditions. CBAM materially supports domestic output in exposed sectors—most notably ferrous metals—by reducing the competitiveness gap with more carbon-intensive imports, while chemicals and cement experience moderate output reductions due to export impacts and demand shifts. Electricity prices emerge as a pivotal determinant of competitiveness in a highly electrified net-zero economy. The enhanced steel module suggests that carbon pricing alone is insufficient for widespread hydrogen-based steelmaking; additional support and/or CCS is required to accelerate breakthrough transitions. Macroeconomically, stringent policies deliver large emissions cuts (≈83% vs. frozen policies by 2050) at a moderate GDP cost (≈1.8%).

title: When moderates endorse extreme means: moral foundations, powerlessness and support for illegal climate action
summary: Abstract Political extremity is commonly attributed to the strength of moral conviction, yet moral conviction also sustains lawful participation. This study asks when moralisation channels citizens towards lawful engagement and when it beco
content: Abstract Political extremity is commonly attributed to the strength of moral conviction, yet moral conviction also sustains lawful participation. This study asks when moralisation channels citizens towards lawful engagement and when it becomes associated with support for illegal means, taking climate change as a case in which both repertoires are active. Drawing on Moral Foundations Theory and the literature on normative and non-normative collective action, a nationally representative online survey of South Korean residents aged 19 and over (June–July 2025; N = 1,970; regression N = 1,895) was analysed using hierarchical regression, modelling support for lawful and for illegal environmental action as distinct outcomes predicted by social solidarity, ideological radicalism and perceived climate injustice, with three binding moral foundations—Purity/Sanctity, Authority and Ingroup loyalty—entered as moderators. The outcomes had different antecedent structures: support for lawful action was associated with collective efficacy, perceived inequality, social trust and intergenerational justice, support for illegal action primarily with powerlessness and anarchism. Of 54 interaction terms, 25 reached p < .05, with small coefficients. Purity/Sanctity and Authority generally attenuated, and in one case reversed, the associations between grievance, ideology and support for illegal action, contradicting the expectation that sacralisation lowers the threshold for extreme means. The single systematic exception was powerlessness, whose association with support for illegal action strengthened as either foundation increased. Extremity therefore arises not from a level of moral conviction but from its conjunction with perceived inefficacy: the boundary between moderate and radical engagement is conditional rather than dispositional, and keeping lawful channels credibly effective is central to governing it.

title: Toward Equilibrium Charges: Environment‐Consistent Atomic Charge Models for Nonpolarizable Force Fields
summary: ABSTRACT Electrostatic interactions in nonpolarizable force fields are represented by fixed atomic charges, despite their sensitivity to molecular environments. We use the self‐consistent polarization (SCP) method to derive environment‐cons
content: ABSTRACT Electrostatic interactions in nonpolarizable force fields are represented by fixed atomic charges, despite their sensitivity to molecular environments. We use the self‐consistent polarization (SCP) method to derive environment‐consistent charges for seven aliphatic alcohols, from methanol to tert‐butanol, in water, methanol, pure alcohol liquids, and n ‐octanol. SCP calculations on MD‐derived solvation clusters reveal solvent‐induced polarization of hydroxyl‐group charges, dominated by direct polarization and environmental back‐polarization. Hydroxyl charges are transferable across alcohols and hydrogen‐bonding solvents, whereas aliphatic carbon and hydrogen charges depend on substitution pattern. SCP‐derived charges improve hydration free energies when transformed from bulk to vacuum values at the water–vacuum interface, achieving mean deviations of c.a. 0.3 kcal mol −1 of experiment. The reproduction of mixing enthalpies for alcohol‐water mixtures was also improved with SCP charges. These results support equilibrium‐derived charges as an intermediate description between additive and explicitly polarizable force fields.

title: Lowering the climate impact of academic conferences: lessons learned from two Swedish cases
summary: Academics, universities and activists increasingly scrutinize academic conferences for their carbon footprints, with questions being raised about the justification for events with very high emissions. This article reports carbon emissions f
content: Academics, universities and activists increasingly scrutinize academic conferences for their carbon footprints, with questions being raised about the justification for events with very high emissions. This article reports carbon emissions from two international academic conferences held in Sweden, with mean per-participant emissions of 0.17 and 0.19 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO2e) (or 0.15 and 0.17 t CO2e, respectively, including virtual participants). Of total calculated emissions, 93% to 95% came from travel (over 80% by air), while accommodation accounted for an estimated 5%. The emissions from digital technology for remote participation were negligible. Emissions were comparatively low in comparison to other international academic conferences. Both events targeted sustainability-related communities and aimed to reduce operational emissions. Our findings suggest three key factors to explain the observed low emissions. First, both conferences had predominantly regional participation, with comparatively few intercontinental attendees (1% and 3%). Second, both conferences were held in locations that are easily accessible by public and land-based transport. Finally, both events offered online participation as an alternative to in-person attendance. This article concludes that conference reach (international vs. regional) has the greatest impact on emissions. For a given geographic extent, organizers should support and promote low-carbon mobility, for example by choosing a conference location with good public, land-based connections and offering meaningful online participation. We also recommend consistently assessing carbon emissions for any academic conference and promoting low-carbon travel for attendees.

title: Modelling the circular economy–renewable integration nexus: a cross-national empirical analysis of smart-technology adoption, territorial CO₂ emissions, and the material footprint
summary: Climate neutrality relies on two levers usually examined separately: circular-economy (CE) practices and renewable integration. Drawing on ecological modernization theory and the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC), we regress per-capita carb
content: Climate neutrality relies on two levers usually examined separately: circular-economy (CE) practices and renewable integration. Drawing on ecological modernization theory and the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC), we regress per-capita carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions in 20 European Union member states over 2014–2023 ( N = 200) on the circular material use (CMU) rate and the renewable energy (REN) share, with smart-technology adoption [ST; internet penetration and research and development (R&D) intensity] as a moderator. The pooled ordinary least squares (OLS), two-way fixed-effects (FE), and random-effects models use cluster-robust standard errors and a wild cluster bootstrap. A 1-percentage-point rise in the renewable energy share is associated with approximately 0.9% lower per-capita emissions in the baseline FE model ( p = 0.095) and 0.95% in the moderated model ( p = 0.030; bootstrap p = 0.048). CMU has no significant unconditional association with emissions in the levels models, and income exhibits concave curvature, although the implied EKC turning point lies above the sample maximum. The CMU × ST interaction is positive and significant ( β = 0.0065, p = 0.009; bootstrap p = 0.033) and is robust across all 20 leave-one-country-out subsamples: the circularity–emissions slope becomes less favourable as adoption rises, with the estimated interaction coefficient larger for internet diffusion than for R&D intensity, although the two estimates cannot be statistically distinguished. Because no conditional slope is individually significant, this association is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a digital-rebound mechanism. For the material footprint outcome, the CMU coefficient is negative, and the interaction changes sign, but neither is significant, so the pattern is specific to production-based CO₂ accounting.

title: Electricity market integration and regional inequality: a research framework for China
summary: Abstract Electricity market integration lowers system costs but redistributes economic opportunity across regions. Whether it narrows or widens regional inequality depends on the balance between two opposing forces: broader access to afford
content: Abstract Electricity market integration lowers system costs but redistributes economic opportunity across regions. Whether it narrows or widens regional inequality depends on the balance between two opposing forces: broader access to affordable electricity that benefits lagging regions, and the concentration of firms and jobs in already advantaged regions. We develop a conceptual framework that links electricity market integration to regional inequality, and we define integration depth as a measurable institutional index distinct from physical transmission capacity. The framework yields four competing trajectories, i.e., declining, inverted-U, U-shaped, and rising inequality, distinguished by observable differences in delivered electricity costs, firm entry, employment, and migration. We further illustrate how Chinese provinces can be grouped along observable dimensions that distinguish these trajectories. Policy should target the mechanism behind an observed distributional outcome rather than assume that integration alone will reduce regional inequality.

title: A magnetically recoverable, fluorescence-tracked, molecularly imprinted nanocarrier for controlled bortezomib release
summary: BACKGROUND: A dual fluorescent-magnetic molecularly imprinted nanocomposite (FMMIP-BTZ) was synthesized by coating Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles with silica and fluorescein-5-isothiocyanate, followed by in-situ polydopamine polymerization using borte
content: BACKGROUND: A dual fluorescent-magnetic molecularly imprinted nanocomposite (FMMIP-BTZ) was synthesized by coating Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles with silica and fluorescein-5-isothiocyanate, followed by in-situ polydopamine polymerization using bortezomib (BTZ) as template. METHODS: The prepared nanocomposite was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), fourier transform infrared (FTIR), UV-visible and fluorescence analysis. RESULTS: Template-selective recognition was confirmed by an imprinting factor of 3.20 (85.34 mg g⁻¹ for FMMIP versus 26.67 mg g⁻¹ for the non-imprinted control), with a BTZ loading efficiency of 69.3%. Release followed zero-order kinetics (k₀ = 3.276% h⁻¹, R² = 0.9937), reaching 80.5 ± 1% cumulative release, and was pH-responsive, rising from 41.1% at pH 7.4 to 84.5% at pH 4 over 6 h. Saturation magnetization fell from 0.48 to 0.04 emu g⁻¹ as the non-magnetic shell was added; despite this, particles remained separable under an external magnetic field at every synthesis, washing, and release step. Dual fluorescence from released BTZ and the FITC-labelled core enabled spectroscopic tracking of release. In an acute dermal irritation assessment, FMMIP-BTZ produced a mean erythema score of 1.00 at 24 h compared with 3.00 for the control. Molecular docking against COX-2, PRDX5, EGFR, and AKT1, together with a 100-ns MD simulation of the AKT1-bortezomib complex, provided exploratory mechanistic context for the experimentally observed response. CONCLUSION: FMMIP-BTZ is thus a molecularly selective, magnetically separable, fluorescence-trackable platform with controlled, pH-responsive release; cellular uptake, cytotoxicity, and in vivo antitumour efficacy remain to be established.

title: Total capacity and spatial distribution of wind and solar power in China under the 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution
summary: Abstract Against the backdrop of global carbon neutrality, the development targets and spatial distribution of renewable capacity such as wind and solar power are key to achieving the goals of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). C
content: Abstract Against the backdrop of global carbon neutrality, the development targets and spatial distribution of renewable capacity such as wind and solar power are key to achieving the goals of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). China’s 2035 NDC target specifies that wind and solar installed capacity should strive to reach 3,600 GW, but its spatial distribution involves multiple coupled constraints—resource endowment, integration space, and energy security—and is a typical cross-domain complex decision-making problem spanning the physical and social systems. Within the cyber-physical-social system in energy (CPSSE) framework, this paper proposes a total-capacity and spatial-allocation method adaptable to different strategic orientations. At the aggregate level, the installed-capacity elastic interval is derived through the coordinated use of NDC emission constraints and the electricity supply–demand framework. At the spatial level, a “strategic weight–resource endowment–integration capacity” three-dimensional correction model is constructed, and regional division is performed based on the cross-domain coupling of the physical and social dimensions. At the engineering level, a truncation-and-redistribution algorithm is introduced to correct the theoretical allocation results under hard constraints. The case results show that the allocation coefficients of the core regions reverse under different strategic orientations and that, after being constrained by physical upper limits, the spillover increment is redistributed to other regions. The method provides a reusable quantitative decision-support tool for medium- and long-term energy planning. Abstract Implications for Energy and Climate Management Abstract Who: National and provincial energy-planning authorities, grid companies, and renewable developers responsible for translating the 2035 NDC target into provincial capacity quotas and project locations. Abstract Management challenge: National targets do not indicate where capacity can actually be built; planners must reconcile strategic priorities with resource endowment, transmission capacity, and land- and sea-use limits, often without a transparent basis for comparing alternatives. Abstract Management implication: Presenting 3,600–4,800 GW as an elastic interval and making the strategic orientation explicit gives decision-makers a reproducible way to compare plans, see which regional limits bind, and anticipate where spillover capacity will land.

title: Postcolonial urbanism without colonies? Rethinking critical urban studies in and from Switzerland
summary: Amid an ongoing public reassessment of the historical legacy of Switzerland's colonial entanglements, this article examines the contested production of knowledge in Swiss geography and urban studies, focusing on the policing of the academy
content: Amid an ongoing public reassessment of the historical legacy of Switzerland's colonial entanglements, this article examines the contested production of knowledge in Swiss geography and urban studies, focusing on the policing of the academy and the epistemic ruptures it has provoked. Tracing historical continuities from radical student movements of the 1980s to recent mobilisations with Black Lives Matter and solidarity with Palestine, we show how moments of dissent have opened spaces for challenging Switzerland's colonial amnesia and racial denial. At the same time, we argue that the political–economic orientation of Swiss critical urban studies, despite its powerful critiques of capitalist urbanisation, has often left the colonial and racial conditions of urbanisation insufficiently examined. Drawing upon historical concepts such as “colonialism without colonies” and “raceless racism”, we conceptualise two mutually reinforcing structures of disavowal: the separation of Swiss modernity and prosperity from colonial histories and the denial of race as an operative social relation despite the persistence of racialised inequalities. This conceptual synthesis enables Swiss urbanisation to be understood relationally through its connections to colonial extraction, racialised mobility, labour segmentation, and global regimes of accumulation. We use postcolonial urban studies not to designate a bounded subfield or category of cities but as a critical practice for reworking the histories, concepts, and methods through which urbanisation is understood. We conclude by advancing an agenda for postcolonial urban studies in and from Switzerland organised around three orientations, namely unmasking space, unearthing extractive geohistories, and unsilencing the everyday, which make racialised spatial relations perceptible, reconstruct the extractive geohistories of urbanisation, and recognise everyday struggles as sites of theorisation.

title: Impact of BRSR on Environmental Disclosure: Evidence from Indian Public and Private Sector Banks
summary: In FY2022-23, the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) became compulsory for India's top 1,000 listed companies. This paper asks whether the new rule changed how much Indian banks disclose about the environment, and whet
content: In FY2022-23, the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) became compulsory for India's top 1,000 listed companies. This paper asks whether the new rule changed how much Indian banks disclose about the environment, and whether it reduced the long-standing gap between public and private sector banks.

title: Scientific, financial, and environmental evaluation of the use of non-ionic surfactants to reduce multi-grade gasoline evaporation loss in tanker trucks under thermodynamic conditions using python simulation
summary: Fuel losses during transportation pose a significant challenge for fuel transportation and distribution agencies. In this study, a chemical method or approach was found to address the state of fuel evaporation, including gasoline, during th
content: Fuel losses during transportation pose a significant challenge for fuel transportation and distribution agencies. In this study, a chemical method or approach was found to address the state of fuel evaporation, including gasoline, during the transportation process. Surfactant materials were used, and this was done by using 100 ppm doses on tanker shipments containing 36,000 liters. A simulation model of mass transfer was developed at temperatures of approximately 60 ° using Python software version 3.14. And depending on API MPMS 19.1 STANDRED BENCHMARK (American petroleum institute manual of petroleum measurement standards). The numerical solution of the governing equations using a time step of ∆t = 0.1 h. Three standard commercial gasoline grades, 87, 91, and 95 octane numbers (ON), were used to compare two surfactants: Span 80 and oleic acid ethoxylate. Regular 87 ON gasoline exhibited the highest natural evaporation rates, as expected. The Span 80 surfactant demonstrated significantly better performance than the alternative, reducing cumulative evaporation by approximately 57,9% and matching the API standards with ≈ ( 1,27), compared to the 63% achieved by oleic acid ethylates. Economically speaking, the treatment essentially pays for itself; a 3.6-liter tank of this material yields about 13,958 Iraqi dinars of super-grade fuel per day. This protective layer mitigates the development of photochemical smog by acting as a chemical barrier that drastically lowers emissions of carcinogenic BTEX gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Crucially, these additives leave no trace and do not affect vehicle engines or fuel combustion efficiency because they are ashless.

title: Coupled and Coordinated Development of New Urbanization and Ecological Vulnerability: Evidence from Counties in the Upper Reaches of the Yangtze River
summary: Abstract Achieving coupled and coordinated development of new urbanization (NU) and ecological vulnerability (EV) is the key to promoting high-quality development. Focusing on 345 counties in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, which ha
content: Abstract Achieving coupled and coordinated development of new urbanization (NU) and ecological vulnerability (EV) is the key to promoting high-quality development. Focusing on 345 counties in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, which have vulnerable ecological condition and experience rapid urbanization in recent years, this study assessed the levels of NU and EV base on multi-dimensional indicator systems, quantitatively analyzed the coupling coordination degree (CCD) between NU and EV from 2010 to 2020 and predicted their future development trends, using entropy weight TOPSIS method, coupling coordination model, Dagum Gini coefficient and ARIMA model with county-level multi-sourced data. The results showed a positive trend of CCD between NU and EV; however, the overall level remains low, and highly vulnerable areas accounted for a large proportion. It is expected that the study area will reach the intermediate CCD between NU and EV by 2030 with intensive ecological recovery and protection measures.

title: Engineering organic–inorganic–polymer hybrid electrolytes for transition bimetallic sulfides@MXene nanocomposites toward advanced energy storage and electrochemical sensing
summary: , a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.015 mM, a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 0.05 mM, and a response time of 3.45 s. The sensor was shown to be highly selective, repeatable, and reproducible, while recovery experiments in simulated plasma a
content: , a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.015 mM, a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 0.05 mM, and a response time of 3.45 s. The sensor was shown to be highly selective, repeatable, and reproducible, while recovery experiments in simulated plasma and pooled human serum verified its suitability for glucose sensing in complex biological matrices. The combination of high-energy storage and sensitive glucose detection reveals the versatility of the VNbS@MXene composite and turns out to be useful in self-powered sensing systems and wearable diagnostic tools of the future.

title: Carbon negative scheduling of direct air capture and hydrogen production in PV powered AI data centers under uncertainty
summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure, exemplified by OpenAI’s data centers, has significantly intensified electricity demand and carbon emissions. To mitigate this environmental impact, this paper propos
content: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure, exemplified by OpenAI’s data centers, has significantly intensified electricity demand and carbon emissions. To mitigate this environmental impact, this paper proposes a novel photovoltaic (PV)-powered microgrid system that integrates Direct Air Capture (DAC) and hydrogen production to simultaneously achieve carbon removal and renewable energy storage. Unlike conventional microgrid scheduling frameworks, this study develops a multi-objective Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) model that addresses uncertain renewable generation, fluctuating electricity prices, and volatile hydrogen and carbon credit markets. The optimization simultaneously minimizes total operational costs, maximizes CO \(_2\) capture efficiency, and ensures hydrogen production aligns with both storage targets and market conditions. The uncertainty modeling is handled by DRO, capturing worst-case deviations within an ambiguity set derived from historical data, ensuring operational resilience. Furthermore, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III) is employed to derive Pareto-optimal trade-offs, providing comprehensive decision support across financial, environmental, and technical dimensions. The proposed optimization framework is applied to a realistic case study modeled on OpenAI’s energy infrastructure. A 100 MW PV farm supplies renewable energy, supported by a 50 MWh battery system and a 60 MW electrolyzer for hydrogen production. The DAC system operates within a 3.5 MW baseline demand, scaling dynamically with surplus solar power. Historical data from NREL, CAISO, EU-ETS, and California hydrogen markets inform the realistic energy prices, carbon credits, and hydrogen values. The optimization is implemented using Pyomo, solved with Gurobi 10.0, and combined with NSGA-III via Platypus. Sensitivity analysis, including Monte Carlo simulations with 10,000 trials, evaluates system resilience under varying solar irradiance, market price volatility, and operational uncertainties. The results demonstrate that PV generation directly governs DAC efficiency and hydrogen production scalability, with clear synchronization between high solar availability and optimal carbon capture performance. Pareto-optimal solutions reveal that increasing CO \(_2\) removal efficiency from 65% to 85% requires a 27% increase in operational costs, highlighting a trade-off between environmental and economic objectives. Furthermore, hydrogen storage utilization peaks at 85% when carbon credit prices surpass $90/ton, indicating strong market-driven operational shifts. Grid dependency reduces by 46% in scenarios prioritizing CO \(_2\) capture, underscoring the system’s ability to enhance renewable self-sufficiency.

title: Activity–selectivity engineering of waste-derived CaO catalysts via KOH and ZnO surface modification for coconut biodiesel production
summary: Abstract The development of sustainable heterogeneous catalysts for biodiesel production requires not only high conversion efficiency, but also precise control over catalytic activity and product selectivity. However, the influence of surfa
content: Abstract The development of sustainable heterogeneous catalysts for biodiesel production requires not only high conversion efficiency, but also precise control over catalytic activity and product selectivity. However, the influence of surface modification on the activity–selectivity balance of waste-derived CaO catalysts remains poorly understood. In this study, eggshell-derived CaO catalysts were chemically modified with KOH and ZnO in order to investigate how surface engineering affects catalytic behaviour during coconut oil transesterification. The catalysts were structurally and compositionally characterised by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and thermogravimetric analysis (TG/DTG), confirming the successful conversion of CaCO₃ into catalytically active CaO, incorporation of potassium- and zinc-containing phases, and significant changes in surface morphology and thermal stability after modification. Under fixed reaction conditions (methanol-to-oil molar ratio of 19:1, 1.5 wt% catalyst, 64°C, 120 min), a clear activity–selectivity trade-off was identified. The KOH-modified catalyst exhibited the highest biodiesel yield (86.9%) and the highest pseudo-first-order kinetic constant (0.0223 min⁻¹), suggesting enhanced catalytic activity and predominantly reaction-controlled behaviour. In contrast, the ZnO-modified catalyst achieved the highest methyl ester content (98.1%) and showed better agreement with pseudo-second-order kinetics, suggesting a greater contribution of adsorption-mediated surface interactions. Biodiesel characterisation by GC-FID, FTIR, TG/DTG, viscosity, and density analyses confirmed the formation of high-quality fatty acid methyl esters compliant with fuel quality standards. Taken together, these findings indicate that chemical modification of waste-derived CaO catalysts enables the rational tuning of catalytic activity and ester selectivity, providing mechanistic insights for the rational design of waste-derived heterogeneous catalysts for sustainable biofuel production within circular economy systems. title: Development of Water Treatment HSSEC System to Support Net Zero Emissions in Maritime Vocational Education: Evidence from Politeknik Pelayaran Sumatera Barat
summary: This study aims to describe the development process of the Water Treatment HSSEC as an initiative to support the achievement of Net Zero Emission at Politeknik Pelayaran Sumatera Barat. The study employed a Research and Development (R&D) me
content: This study aims to describe the development process of the Water Treatment HSSEC as an initiative to support the achievement of Net Zero Emission at Politeknik Pelayaran Sumatera Barat. The study employed a Research and Development (R&D) method using the ADDIE development model, which was limited to the analysis and design phases. The analysis phase included curriculum analysis based on the IMO Model Course 7.04 Officer in Charge of an Engineering Watch using an observation checklist, lecturers' needs analysis through semi-structured interviews, and students' needs analysis using a questionnaire covering the dimensions of necessity, lack, and want. The findings revealed that the existing curriculum has not comprehensively integrated Water Treatment HSSEC into the learning process, practical learning media and instructional materials remain limited, and both lecturers and students expressed a strong need for learning media that support Green Shipping and Net Zero Emission. The design phase produced a Water Treatment HSSEC prototype consisting of a multi-stage filtration system, water circulation mechanism, concrete filtration tank, and a manual book containing the conceptual framework, system architecture, filtration mechanism, standard operating procedures, maintenance guidelines, and occupational safety procedures. The results indicate that the proposed Water Treatment HSSEC has been designed in accordance with user needs, the characteristics of maritime vocational education, and the demands of the shipping industry, thereby demonstrating its potential to serve as a Teaching Factory that enhances students' competencies while supporting the implementation of Net Zero Emission at Politeknik Pelayaran Sumatera Barat.

title: Failing great expectations: Systemic assessment of the technological and economic viability of commercial fusion undertakings
summary: Start-ups and governments have great expectations about the future of energy from fusion, like imminent roll-out at scale, abundance, low cost and negligible environmental impact. Most start-ups claim to be in the final stages of building a
content: Start-ups and governments have great expectations about the future of energy from fusion, like imminent roll-out at scale, abundance, low cost and negligible environmental impact. Most start-ups claim to be in the final stages of building a fully functional fusion power plant. The aim of this study is to assess these narratives and the communicated expectations around fusion energy. These clear narratives are compared with the state of knowledge, the low technical maturity of essential processes, and the pending integration of interacting and parallel processes into an extremely complex fusion energy system. Narratives of a benign or sustainable technology are related to immense resource and energy needs. Promises of abundance at low cost are placed in perspective of inherent complexity and resource demand. This study is unable to support the great expectations set forth by these start-ups and governments. Meeting the technical needs of a reliable and cost-effective power plant with fusion seems exceptionally unlikely, as research still does not provide basic answers for essential engineering. A fusion energy system will not be clean, carbon-neutral or benign. Cost of fusion power will in view of the immense resource demand substantially exceed the cost of renewable or fission power. Metal availability constrains any energy system and would severely limit fusion power capacity, well below abundance. As these factors impede the economic viability of fusion power, this study seeks possible alternative viable business models of fusion start-ups and political narratives, outside of creating a fusion power plant.

title: Research on Systematic Optimization and Improvement Methods for Voltage Quality in Distribution Networks with High-Penetration Distributed Generation
summary: Abstract This paper develops a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) controller for voltage quality in distribution networks with high-penetration distributed generation. Each photovoltaic inverter acts as an autonomous agent that
content: Abstract This paper develops a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) controller for voltage quality in distribution networks with high-penetration distributed generation. Each photovoltaic inverter acts as an autonomous agent that controls its reactive power from local measurements, while a QMIX-style mixing network is used during centralized training to decompose the global reward. The reward combines voltage deviation, network loss, a security barrier and action smoothness. The method is evaluated on the IEEE 33-bus feeder with six PV units, 15-min resolution, 50–75% penetration, three load levels and four operating scenarios (normal, communication delay, sensor data loss and PV tripping). Compared with no control, the controller raises the voltage qualification rate from 91.0% to 100% and reduces the average voltage deviation by 12.7% and the daily network loss by 14.8%; compared with droop control it attains the same qualification rate with a 1.9% lower daily loss. Among VDN, IQL, MADDPG and the proposed method, the four learned controllers reach nearly the same operating point; QMIX-CTDE is competitive with the best baseline, which shows that the proposed reward design and the decentralized execution architecture, rather than a particular value-decomposition variant, determine the performance. Batch experiments over 36 operating conditions show that the decentralized policy degrades gracefully when measurements or actuators are lost. The results provide a reproducible benchmark and practical evidence for deploying decentralized voltage control in high-DG distribution networks.

title: Waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors: fundamentals, advances, and insights
summary: Photodetectors that integrate two-dimensional (2D) materials with optical waveguides are considered an ideal approach to enhance infrared detection capability and on-chip integration capability and have become a focal point of recent resear
content: Photodetectors that integrate two-dimensional (2D) materials with optical waveguides are considered an ideal approach to enhance infrared detection capability and on-chip integration capability and have become a focal point of recent research. These devices benefit not only from the intrinsic optoelectronic properties and flexible hetero-integration of 2D materials but also from a range of engineering strategies that enable precise control over their electronic and optical characteristics. In addition, by combining different types of waveguide structures, the optical field distribution can be effectively tailored, further strengthening light-matter interactions and facilitating the realization of compact, high-performance infrared photodetectors with versatile strategies. This review systematically summarizes the latest progress in waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors, organized primarily by the type of waveguide material and further categorized according to the 2D materials employed. It discusses the advantages of various waveguide structures and 2D materials, the working mechanisms, performance parameters, common device architectures, and many key approaches to improving photodetector performance (e.g., waveguide structure optimization, electrode material and spacing design, gate electrostatic doping, substrate engineering, strain modulation, twist angle control of 2D materials, heterojunction band alignment, etc). Furthermore, a comparative analysis with conventional commercial photodetectors is provided, demonstrating that waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors have already achieved comparable performance in many applications, while certain challenges remain. Finally, the review outlines the key obstacles facing practical implementation and offers perspectives on future research directions.

title: Integrated Decarbonization Pathways for Pakistan's Transport Sector: A Multi-Pollutant Assessment of Policy Synergies
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Pakistan’s transport sector is a rapidly growing source of greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants, posing significant challenges for achieving carbon neutrality while safeguarding public health and energy security. This study develops
content: Pakistan’s transport sector is a rapidly growing source of greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants, posing significant challenges for achieving carbon neutrality while safeguarding public health and energy security. This study develops a technology-resolved emission inventory for 2024 and evaluates mitigation pathways to 2050 using an integrated assessment framework that links bottom-up emissions modeling with energy demand projections and policy scenario analysis. The framework enables a consistent assessment of sectoral decarbonization pathways alongside co-benefits for air quality. The analysis covers major pollutant groups, including particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), carbon monoxide (CO), and carbon dioxide (CO₂), across road and non-road transport modes. Four scenarios are assessed: a Business-as-Usual (BAU) pathway, an Electric Vehicle Transition (EVT), implementation of Euro-VI emission standards, and an integrated policy package aligned with enhanced national climate commitments (NDC+), representing a pathway toward transport sector decarbonization. Results indicate that road transport accounts for over 97% of total sectoral emissions, highlighting its central role in mitigation strategies. Heavy-duty diesel vehicles dominate PM and NOₓ emissions, whereas passenger cars and two- and three-wheelers are the primary contributors to CO₂ emissions. Under BAU, emissions increase substantially through 2050, diverging from carbon neutrality objectives. Mitigation scenarios show that electrification is critical for deep CO₂ reductions, while Euro-VI standards deliver rapid improvements in air quality. The integrated NDC+ scenario achieves the most substantial overall emission reductions, demonstrating the importance of combining technology shifts with regulatory measures. These findings underscore that achieving carbon neutrality in the transport sector requires coordinated, multi-policy strategies rather than isolated interventions. The study contributes to sectoral integrated assessment literature by providing a policy-relevant framework for evaluating low-carbon transport transitions in emerging economies.
